name: Milk facial

lead: A milk facial applies milk to the face, a beauty custom with long roots in milk bathing. It is used for a smoother, brighter-looking, paler complexion.

Wikipedia describes milk baths as working through lactic acid, an alpha hydroxy acid that loosens bonds between dead skin cells. Historical stories link milk to Cleopatra, Poppaea and Elizabeth I, and to singer Anna Held in the early 1900s [1].

paras: Milk is applied to the face or used in a bath. Buttermilk, yogurt and milk powders are variants.
Skin that reacts to dairy or acids may be irritated. No clinical trials of milk facials are cited here.

chain: Lactic acid loosens dead surface cells
angle.text: People apply milk for a soft, glowing complexion, with lactic acid giving mild exfoliation.

lead: A milk facial applies milk to the skin for a smoother, brighter complexion. It descends from the older custom of milk baths [1].

Wikipedia says milk baths use lactic acid, an alpha hydroxy acid that dissolves proteins holding dead skin cells together [1]. It reports unconfirmed legends of Cleopatra bathing in donkey milk, historian Adrian Goldsworthy's view that Poppaea started the fashion, Tudor queens bathing in milk for younger, paler skin, and Anna Held's publicized milk baths [1].

paras: Claudette Colbert's 1932 and 1934 film roles as Poppaea and Cleopatra helped tie milk baths to Cleopatra in popular memory [1]. Anna Held was reported to bathe in milk daily, later saying twice a week, and husband Florenz Ziegfeld Jr. publicized deliveries [1].

timeline.event: Film portrayals of Poppaea and Cleopatra popularize milk bathing [1]
